[Gilles Deleuze](/thoughts/Gilles-Deleuze) and Félix Guattari develop the rhizome in _A Thousand Plateaus_, part of [Capitalism and Schizophrenia](/thoughts/Gilles-Deleuze#capitalism-and-schizophrenia). It describes connections that can cross between different kinds of things without following a single hierarchy. The arrangement has multiple entryways and can change as new connections form.[^source]

Their orchid and wasp example makes this concrete. The orchid attracts the wasp; the wasp transports its pollen. Their connection crosses the plant–animal division through what they do together. A classification that places them on separate branches leaves out this interaction.

A rhizome can still contain hierarchies. Deleuze and Guattari explicitly include organized segments and tree-like structures within it. Those arrangements can acquire new connections or be reorganized. Describing a rhizome as free of _all_ structure loses this part of the account: the existing organization matters because it shapes where connections develop and where they are blocked.

[^source]: Deleuze and Guattari, [_A Thousand Plateaus_](https://files.libcom.org/files/A%20Thousand%20Plateaus.pdf), translated by Brian Massumi (1987), “Introduction: Rhizome,” pp. 7–21. See p. 10 for the orchid and wasp, pp. 9 and 15 for organization within rhizomes, and p. 20 for hierarchies.
